# 12-Week Resistance & Metabolic Health Programme

### Client Profile Summary
**Age:** 31 | **Sex:** Female | **Condition:** PCOS (Rotterdam criteria) | **HbA1c:** 5.8% (pre-diabetic range) | **BMI:** 28 | **Cycle status:** Irregular, partially anovulatory | **Clearance:** Full exercise, endocrinologist-directed resistance training as first-line therapy

---

## Overarching Design Philosophy

Before the week-by-week detail, it is worth explaining the reasoning behind every structural decision, because this client's endocrine picture demands more nuance than a standard body-composition block.

**Why resistance training is the primary tool.** Skeletal muscle is the largest site of insulin-mediated glucose disposal in the body. Progressive resistance training increases GLUT-4 transporter density and improves post-receptor insulin signalling independently of weight loss. For a woman with PCOS and a borderline HbA1c, this is not a cosmetic choice — it is metabolic medicine. Every session is therefore built around compound, multi-joint movements that recruit the largest possible muscle mass.

**Why excessive cardio is avoided.** Chronic high-volume aerobic work elevates cortisol, suppresses LH pulsatility, and worsens HPA-axis dysregulation — all of which are already problematic in PCOS. Cardio is included in a supporting role only: short, purposeful sessions that improve cardiovascular efficiency and insulin sensitivity without creating a catabolic hormonal environment.

**Why the programme is periodised in three phases rather than linear.** An irregular cycle means this client cannot reliably use menstrual phase-based periodisation. Instead, the programme uses a load-volume periodisation model with built-in deload weeks, which manages cumulative fatigue and cortisol load regardless of where she is hormonally on any given week.

**Why under-fuelling is explicitly prohibited.** Caloric restriction beyond roughly 15–20% below maintenance in women with PCOS suppresses GnRH pulsatility, raises cortisol, and can worsen insulin resistance — the opposite of the therapeutic goal. The nutrition framework therefore targets a modest, sustainable deficit or even maintenance calories in the early weeks, with protein as the non-negotiable anchor.

---

## Programme Architecture at a Glance

| Phase | Weeks | Primary Goal | Training Days/Week | Dominant Rep Range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 — Foundation | 1–4 | Movement quality, metabolic priming | 3 | 10–15 |
| 2 — Hypertrophy | 5–8 | Muscle mass, progressive overload | 4 | 8–12 |
| 3 — Strength-Hypertrophy | 9–12 | Strength, body composition consolidation | 4 | 5–10 |

**Session structure every week:** Resistance training sessions are 50–65 minutes. Each session includes a 5-minute warm-up, the main block, and a 5-minute cool-down. Cardio sessions are 20–30 minutes, low-to-moderate intensity, on separate days or as a short post-lifting addition only in Phase 1.

**Deload weeks:** Weeks 4, 8, and 12 are structured deloads — volume drops by approximately 40%, intensity drops by 10–15%, and the focus shifts to movement quality and recovery. These are not optional rest weeks; they are programmed adaptations.

---

## Nutrition Framework

*Note to trainer: refer the client to a registered dietitian with PCOS experience for individualised targets. The following is a framework to guide training-day and rest-day fuelling.*

**Caloric target:** Aim for maintenance calories in Weeks 1–4 while the client adapts to training. From Week 5 onward, a modest deficit of 200–300 kcal/day is appropriate if body composition is the goal — no more. This is not a crash diet. Remind the client that the muscle she is building is metabolically active tissue that will improve insulin sensitivity around the clock.

**Protein:** This is the single most important nutritional variable. Target **1.8–2.2 g per kg of bodyweight per day**. At a BMI of 28 and an estimated bodyweight of approximately 72–78 kg (adjust to actual), this means roughly **130–170 g protein daily**. Protein is distributed across at least four meals to maximise muscle protein synthesis. High protein intake also improves satiety without suppressing hormones the way aggressive caloric restriction does.

**Carbohydrates:** Do not eliminate carbohydrates. Carbohydrate timing around training is a powerful tool for insulin sensitivity — consuming the majority of daily carbohydrates in the two-hour window around training sessions (pre and post) improves glucose disposal and supports performance. Prioritise low-glycaemic, fibre-rich sources: oats, legumes, sweet potato, brown rice, vegetables, berries. Target approximately **3–4 g/kg on training days** and **2–3 g/kg on rest days**.

**Fats:** Adequate dietary fat is essential for steroidogenesis and hormone production. Do not drop fat below 0.8–1 g/kg. Prioritise omega-3 sources (oily fish, walnuts, flaxseed) given their anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitising properties. There is reasonable evidence that omega-3 supplementation (2–3 g EPA+DHA daily) is beneficial in PCOS specifically.

**Key supplements with evidence in PCOS:**
- **Inositol (myo-inositol 2 g + D-chiro-inositol 50 mg, 40:1 ratio):** Strong evidence for improving insulin sensitivity and ovarian function in PCOS. Recommend discussing with endocrinologist.
- **Vitamin D:** Deficiency is extremely common in PCOS and worsens insulin resistance. Test and supplement to achieve serum 25-OH-D above 50 nmol/L.
- **Magnesium glycinate (300–400 mg at night):** Supports insulin signalling, sleep quality, and HPA-axis regulation.
- **Creatine monohydrate (3–5 g/day):** Emerging evidence for improving insulin sensitivity and body composition in women; well-tolerated and safe.

**Meal timing on training days:** Eat a mixed meal (protein + carbohydrate + small amount of fat) 60–90 minutes before training. Within 30–60 minutes post-training, consume a protein-rich snack or meal (at least 30–40 g protein) alongside carbohydrates to maximise the insulin-sensitising window that resistance exercise opens.

**What to avoid:** Skipping meals, intermittent fasting protocols beyond a natural overnight fast, very low-carbohydrate diets (these can raise cortisol in women with HPA dysfunction), and ultra-processed foods high in refined sugar and trans fats.

---

## Recovery Framework

**Sleep:** This is non-negotiable. Poor sleep acutely worsens insulin resistance and raises cortisol. Target 7–9 hours. Discuss sleep hygiene if the client reports difficulty — magnesium supplementation at night, consistent sleep/wake times, and limiting screens before bed are first-line strategies.

**Stress management:** Chronic psychological stress is a major driver of HPA dysfunction in PCOS. Encourage the client to identify her primary stressors. Even 10 minutes of daily diaphragmatic breathing or mindfulness practice has measurable effects on cortisol. This is not soft advice — it is endocrine management.

**Active recovery:** On rest days, encourage low-intensity movement: walking (20–30 minutes), gentle yoga, or swimming. These improve insulin sensitivity without creating a cortisol burden.

**Soreness management:** Expect significant DOMS in Weeks 1–2. Encourage adequate hydration, protein intake, and sleep rather than NSAIDs (which can blunt some adaptation signalling). Foam rolling and light stretching are appropriate.

**Tracking:** Ask the client to log subjective energy, mood, and sleep quality on a simple 1–10 scale each morning. This is an early warning system for overtraining and HPA stress. If scores drop consistently below 5 for three or more consecutive days, reduce training volume that week regardless of the programme schedule.

---

---

# PHASE 1 — FOUNDATION (Weeks 1–4)

## Phase 1 Goals
Establish movement competency in the six fundamental patterns (hinge, squat, push, pull, carry, core anti-rotation). Prime the metabolic system with consistent training stimulus. Build the habit of training three days per week without creating excessive fatigue. Introduce the client to RPE-based effort regulation, which is more appropriate than percentage-based loading at this stage because her baseline strength is unknown.

**RPE guide for this client:** RPE 6 = could do 4+ more reps easily. RPE 7 = could do 3 more reps. RPE 8 = could do 2 more reps. RPE 9 = could do 1 more rep. Never exceed RPE 8 in Phase 1.

**Training split:** Full-body, three days per week (e.g., Monday / Wednesday / Friday, or Tuesday / Thursday / Saturday). At least one full rest day between sessions.

---

## Week 1 (1 June – 7 June 2026)

**Theme:** Learn the movements. Load is light. The goal is to finish each session feeling energised, not depleted. RPE cap: 6–7 on all working sets.

### Session A (Monday 1 June) — Full Body, Movement Introduction

**Warm-up (5 minutes):** 2 minutes light cycling or rowing, then: 10 bodyweight squats, 10 glute bridges, 10 band pull-aparts, 10 cat-cows, 5 inchworms.

**Main Block:**

*A1. Goblet Squat* — 3 sets × 12 reps. Hold a light dumbbell (8–12 kg to start) at the chest. Focus on keeping the chest tall, knees tracking over toes, and reaching depth comfortably. Rest 90 seconds between sets. This is the foundational squat pattern and also an excellent core stability exercise.

*B1. Romanian Deadlift (Dumbbell)* — 3 sets × 12 reps. Two dumbbells, hip-width stance. Hinge at the hip, maintaining a neutral spine, feeling a stretch in the hamstrings. Do not round the lower back. This is the hinge pattern and directly targets the posterior chain — the largest muscle group in the body and a major site of glucose disposal. Rest 90 seconds.

*C1. Dumbbell Bench Press* — 3 sets × 12 reps. Moderate weight. Full range of motion, controlled eccentric (3-second lowering). Rest 90 seconds.

*C2. Seated Cable Row (or Dumbbell Bent-Over Row)* — 3 sets × 12 reps. Superset with C1, rest 60 seconds between exercises. Pull the elbows back, squeeze the shoulder blades together at the end of the movement.

*D1. Dumbbell Overhead Press (Seated or Standing)* — 2 sets × 12 reps. Light weight. Brace the core, avoid excessive lumbar extension. Rest 90 seconds.

*E1. Plank* — 3 sets × 20–30 seconds. Focus on a rigid body position — do not let the hips sag or pike. Rest 45 seconds.

**Cool-down (5 minutes):** Hip flexor stretch (60 seconds each side), hamstring stretch, thoracic rotation, child's pose.

---

### Session B (Wednesday 3 June) — Full Body, Pattern Reinforcement

**Warm-up (5 minutes):** Same as Session A, or substitute 5 minutes of light rowing.

**Main Block:**

*A1. Leg Press* — 3 sets × 15 reps. Feet shoulder-width, moderate depth. This is a lower-skill alternative to the squat that allows higher loading of the quadriceps and glutes with less technical demand. Useful in early weeks to build confidence and volume. Rest 90 seconds.

*B1. Dumbbell Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift* — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg. Hold one dumbbell in the opposite hand to the working leg. This challenges balance and hip stability. Use a wall or rack for light support if needed in Week 1. Rest 90 seconds.

*C1. Lat Pulldown (Wide Grip)* — 3 sets × 12 reps. Pull the bar to the upper chest, leading with the elbows. This builds the latissimus dorsi, which is important for posture and upper-body pulling strength. Rest 90 seconds.

*C2. Dumbbell Lateral Raise* — 3 sets × 15 reps. Light weight. Controlled movement, slight bend in the elbow. Superset with C1, rest 60 seconds between exercises.

*D1. Hip Thrust (Bodyweight or Barbell — light)* — 3 sets × 15 reps. Drive through the heels, squeeze the glutes at the top. The glutes are the largest muscle in the body; training them directly is a significant metabolic stimulus. Rest 90 seconds.

*E1. Dead Bug* — 3 sets × 8 reps each side. Slow and controlled. Opposite arm and leg extend simultaneously while the lower back stays pressed into the floor. Excellent for deep core stability and spinal control.

**Cool-down:** Same as Session A.

---

### Session C (Friday 5 June) — Full Body, Introduce Carries and Unilateral Work

**Warm-up (5 minutes):** 5 minutes light treadmill walk at incline, then band work as above.

**Main Block:**

*A1. Dumbbell Split Squat (Rear Foot Elevated — Bulgarian, or standard split squat if balance is a challenge)* — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg. This is a high-value unilateral exercise that corrects left-right imbalances and loads the glutes and quads heavily. Start with bodyweight or very light dumbbells. Rest 90 seconds per leg.

*B1. Trap Bar Deadlift (or Conventional Barbell Deadlift — light)* — 3 sets × 10 reps. The trap bar is preferred in early weeks because it reduces shear force on the lumbar spine and is more intuitive for beginners. Load conservatively — the goal is perfect mechanics. Rest 2 minutes.

*C1. Cable Chest Fly or Pec Deck* — 2 sets × 15 reps. Isolation work to reinforce the chest pattern. Rest 60 seconds.

*C2. Face Pull (Cable, rope attachment)* — 2 sets × 15 reps. Pull to the face, external rotation at the end. Excellent for shoulder health and posture. Superset with C1.

*D1. Farmer's Carry* — 3 sets × 30 metres. Hold a dumbbell in each hand (moderate weight — challenging but not maximal). Walk with a tall posture, braced core. Carries are one of the most functional and metabolically demanding exercises available. Rest 90 seconds.

*E1. Pallof Press (Cable or Band)* — 3 sets × 10 reps each side. Anti-rotation core exercise. Stand side-on to the cable, press the handle straight out and hold for 2 seconds. This trains the core to resist rotation — a critical function for spinal health.

**Cool-down:** Full-body stretch, 5 minutes.

---

**Week 1 Cardio:** One optional 20-minute walk at a comfortable pace on a rest day (Saturday or Sunday). Do not add more than this in Week 1.

---

## Week 2 (8 June – 14 June 2026)

**Theme:** Repeat the same three sessions as Week 1 with a small increase in load (approximately 5% on lower body, 2.5–5% on upper body where technique allows). Add one set to the main compound movements (goblet squat, RDL, trap bar deadlift, hip thrust). RPE cap remains 7. The client should be feeling more comfortable with the movements and beginning to develop proprioceptive awareness.

**Session A:** Add 1 set to goblet squat (now 4 × 12) and RDL (now 4 × 12). Increase load by 5% if Week 1 felt easy (RPE was below 6).

**Session B:** Add 1 set to leg press (now 4 × 15) and hip thrust (now 4 × 15). Introduce a light barbell to the hip thrust if bodyweight is no longer challenging.

**Session C:** Add 1 set to trap bar deadlift (now 4 × 10). Increase farmer's carry weight slightly or extend distance to 40 metres.

**Cardio:** Add one 20-minute low-intensity steady-state session (cycling, rowing, or walking) on a rest day. Keep heart rate below 65% of maximum (approximately 120–125 bpm for a 31-year-old). This is not a fat-burning session — it is an insulin-sensitising, recovery-enhancing session.

---

## Week 3 (15 June – 21 June 2026)

**Theme:** Progressive overload continues. Introduce tempo manipulation to increase time under tension, which is a powerful driver of hypertrophy and metabolic adaptation without requiring heavier loads. All compound movements this week use a **3-1-1 tempo** (3-second eccentric, 1-second pause, 1-second concentric). This will feel significantly harder at the same load — do not increase weight this week. RPE cap: 7–8.

**Session A:** Goblet squat 4 × 10 at 3-1-1 tempo. RDL 4 × 10 at 3-1-1 tempo. Bench press 3 × 10 at 3-1-1 tempo. Cable row 3 × 12. Overhead press 3 × 10. Plank 3 × 30–40 seconds.

**Session B:** Leg press 4 × 12 at 3-1-1 tempo. Single-leg RDL 3 × 10 each side. Lat pulldown 3 × 12 at 3-1-1 tempo. Lateral raise 3 × 15. Hip thrust 4 × 12 at 3-1-1 tempo. Dead bug 3 × 10 each side.

**Session C:** Bulgarian split squat 3 × 10 each leg at 3-1-1 tempo. Trap bar deadlift 4 × 8 at 3-1-1 tempo. Cable fly 2 × 15. Face pull 3 × 15. Farmer's carry 3 × 40 metres. Pallof press 3 × 10 each side.

**Cardio:** Two 20-minute low-intensity sessions on rest days.

---

## Week 4 — Deload (22 June – 28 June 2026)

**Theme:** Active recovery. Volume drops by 40%. Load drops by 10–15%. Three sessions still occur, but they are shorter (40 minutes maximum) and feel easy. This is not laziness — it is when the adaptations from Weeks 1–3 consolidate. Skipping the deload is the most common mistake in programming and leads to accumulated fatigue that blunts progress.

**All three sessions this week:** Perform the same exercises as the corresponding session from Week 1, but reduce to 2 sets per exercise, reduce load by 10–15%, and use a normal tempo (no 3-1-1). RPE cap: 5–6. The client should leave each session feeling refreshed.

**Cardio:** One 25-minute walk. No additional cardio.

**Recovery focus this week:** Prioritise sleep. Encourage the client to reflect on how her body feels, note any persistent soreness or fatigue, and discuss nutrition adherence. This is also a good week to take baseline measurements (bodyweight, waist circumference, hip circumference, and optionally a DEXA scan if available) to track body composition progress.

# PHASE 2 — HYPERTROPHY (Weeks 5–8)

## Phase 2 Goals
Increase training frequency to four days per week using an upper/lower split. Increase total weekly volume (sets per muscle group) to drive hypertrophy. Hypertrophy is the primary mechanism by which resistance training improves insulin sensitivity — more muscle mass means more GLUT-4 transporters and a larger glucose sink. Rep ranges shift to 8–12 for most exercises. RPE progresses to 7–8 on working sets, with occasional sets at RPE 9 in the final week of the phase.

**Training split:** Upper A / Lower A / Rest / Upper B / Lower B / Rest / Rest (or adjust to client's schedule, maintaining at least one rest day between upper and lower sessions).

---

## Week 5 (29 June – 5 July 2026)

**Theme:** Introduce the upper/lower split. The client will notice the increased frequency and volume. Emphasise that this is intentional and that nutrition (especially protein and carbohydrate around sessions) is critical to support recovery. RPE: 7–8 on main lifts.

### Upper A — Horizontal Push/Pull Focus

**Warm-up:** 5 minutes rowing, band pull-aparts × 15, shoulder circles, thoracic extension over foam roller.

*A1. Barbell Bench Press* — 4 sets × 10 reps. This is the first time the barbell bench press is introduced. Spot the client on the first session. Focus on a stable arch, feet flat on the floor, bar path slightly diagonal. Rest 2 minutes.

*B1. Barbell Bent-Over Row* — 4 sets × 10 reps. Hinge to approximately 45 degrees, pull the bar to the lower chest/upper abdomen. This is a high-value compound pull that also challenges the posterior chain isometrically. Rest 2 minutes.

*C1. Incline Dumbbell Press* — 3 sets × 12 reps. 30–45 degree incline. Targets the upper chest and anterior deltoid. Rest 90 seconds.

*C2. Seated Cable Row (Close Grip)* — 3 sets × 12 reps. Superset with C1. Rest 60 seconds between exercises.

*D1. Dumbbell Lateral Raise* — 3 sets × 15 reps. Rest 60 seconds.

*D2. Rear Delt Fly (Dumbbell or Cable)* — 3 sets × 15 reps. Superset with D1.

*E1. Tricep Pushdown (Cable)* — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 60 seconds.

*E2. Dumbbell Bicep Curl* — 3 sets × 12 reps. Superset with E1.

**Cool-down:** Upper body stretch, 5 minutes.

---

### Lower A — Quad-Dominant Focus

**Warm-up:** 5 minutes cycling, glute bridges × 15, leg swings, hip circles, bodyweight squats × 10.

*A1. Barbell Back Squat* — 4 sets × 8 reps. This is the introduction of the barbell back squat. Spend extra time on warm-up sets (bar × 10, then 50% working weight × 5, then 75% × 3 before working sets). The back squat is the single most metabolically demanding exercise in this programme and a cornerstone of insulin sensitivity training. Rest 2–3 minutes between working sets.

*B1. Romanian Deadlift (Barbell)* — 4 sets × 10 reps. Transition from dumbbell to barbell RDL. Allows heavier loading and greater hamstring stimulus. Rest 2 minutes.

*C1. Leg Press* — 3 sets × 12 reps. Higher foot placement to emphasise glutes and hamstrings. Rest 90 seconds.

*C2. Leg Curl (Machine, Lying or Seated)* — 3 sets × 12 reps. Superset with C1. Isolates the hamstrings. Rest 60 seconds between exercises.

*D1. Walking Lunge (Dumbbell)* — 3 sets × 12 reps each leg. Challenges balance, hip stability, and quad/glute strength simultaneously. Rest 90 seconds.

*E1. Calf Raise (Machine or Smith Machine)* — 3 sets × 15 reps. Rest 60 seconds.
